title: Contouring mitigates voiding at the lithium/ceramic electrolyte interface on discharging solid-state batteries - Nature Energy
byline: Zhang; Shengming; Hu; Bingkun; Melvin; Dominic L R; Spencer-Jolly; Gao; Xiangwen; Wang; Longlong; Yang; Lechen; Monroe; Charles W; Bruce; Peter G
html:
Abstract

Interfacial void formation during discharge limits the practical performance of lithium metal solid-state batteries. Here we show that introducing an egg-box topography at the Li/Li6PS5Cl interface increases the discharge current at which voiding commences tenfold, from 0.2 to 2 mA cm−2 at 2 MPa and 30 °C. The contoured interface also sustains pulsed currents up to 3 mA cm−2 at 30 °C and 8 mA cm−2 at 60 °C without cell failure. Under these conditions, it does not completely eliminate void formation but suppresses void growth and associated voltage polarization. Consequently, it sustains discharge profiles derived from the Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Procedure, representing realistic electric vehicle driving demands, whereas non-contoured interfaces fail rapidly. A full cell with a thin contoured solid electrolyte retains this advantage over its non-contoured counterpart. Contouring the Li/solid electrolyte interface is therefore an effective strategy for enabling practically relevant discharge rates in solid-state batteries.

Main

Voids can form at the lithium/ceramic electrolyte interface during the discharge of solid-state batteries, leading to increased polarization and ultimately cell failure1,2. Voiding occurs when the flux of Li+ away from the interface through the solid electrolyte exceeds the rate at which Li can be transported to the interface within the anode3,4,5. Because of the resulting reduction in contact area, leading to increased local current density during subsequent charging6,7, voiding can also initiate dendrite formation at lower charging currents, ultimately leading to short circuit and cell failure8,9,10. The recognition of this fact has led to considerable focus on the voiding problem in recent years11,12,13,14,15.

Voiding can be alleviated to some extent by applying a sufficiently high stack pressure (for example, >10 MPa) such that the creep rate of lithium is enough to match the discharge current density16,17. However, practical solid-state batteries are very unlikely to operate at such high stack pressures; typically, ≤2 MPa will be required. The challenge is how to mitigate voiding at practical discharge currents without high pressures. To date, approaches have included: forming lithium-based alloys in an attempt to access higher Li transport rates within the anode18,19,20,21,22, the introduction of interlayers between the lithium metal and the ceramic electrolyte, again to improve Li mass transport to the interface23,24,25,26, and the formation of 3D architectures of mixed ionic- and electronic- conductors within the anode27,28.

An alternative, which requires no new materials, alloys or interlayers, is to contour the interface, that is, to impose a periodic 3D topography on the Li/ceramic electrolyte interface. For a given discharge current, the larger interfacial area should reduce the local current density, enabling higher discharge rates before voiding occurs. However, contouring also introduces heterogeneity in the current density distribution, and regions of higher local current are where voiding is most likely to begin. Contouring has been explored for mitigating dendrites on charging29,30,31, and we showed previously that it increases the charging current at which dendrites occur, by only a modest degree, less than 50%, too little to provide a viable solution to the problem of dendrites29. However, little or no attention has been given to the effect contouring might have on stripping and whether it can alleviate voiding. Given that voiding arises from the flux imbalance of Li and Li+ at the interface, a very different mechanism from dendrites on charging, the effect of contouring on discharge performance cannot be assumed to follow that seen for charging.

Here we contour the Li/Li6PS5Cl interface by 3D templating and examine its effect on voiding during discharge. At 2 MPa and 30 °C, contouring increases the discharge current at which voiding commences tenfold, from 0.2 to 2 mA cm−2. In practice, cells are rarely discharged at a constant current throughout the whole discharge, therefore we also examined the effect of pulse discharge. Under pulsed conditions at 2 MPa, the contoured interface sustains currents of 3 mA cm−2 at 30 °C and 8 mA cm−2 at 60 °C. It also sustains a discharge sequence derived from the Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Procedure (WLTP), in which current peaks reach 9 mA cm−2, whereas a non-contoured interface fails. A full cell with an 80 µm contoured Li6PS5Cl electrolyte and a LiNi0.83Mn0.06Co0.11O2 composite cathode cycles stably at a discharge current of 6 mA cm−2 at 2 MPa and 60 °C, whereas the corresponding non-contoured cell fails during the second charge. Our findings show that contouring has a substantial effect on the discharge of solid-state batteries with lithium metal anodes and ceramic electrolytes, sustaining higher constant and pulsed discharge currents and completing the WLTP discharge sequence.

Optimizing the contour geometry

The variation of current density across a contoured Li/solid electrolyte (SE) interface, and consequently the maximum local current density (where voids will form), depends on the topography of the interface. Previously, we calculated the current distribution for three topographies, frustums of square pyramids, egg box and square pyramids29 (Fig. 1a), and for the same applied discharge current, the maximum local current is lowest for the egg-box topography29 (Supplementary Fig. 1). High local currents occur at sudden changes in direction across the surface, that is, sharp corners, which the sinusoidal shape of the egg-box topography avoids. To measure the critical current of stripping (CCS) for the three topographies, 3D-printed polymer templates were pressed onto Argyrodite, Li6PS5Cl, powder in a die set, transferring the topography onto the Li6PS5Cl disc; the template was then removed, the solid electrolyte sintered and the lithium anode attached. The CCS was measured using three-electrode cells to avoid any influence from polarization at the counter electrode. Throughout this work, voiding was judged to have commenced when the voltage polarization grew by 2 mV during stripping (Supplementary Fig. 2). The CCS is highest for the egg-box topography (Fig. 1b), consistent with it having the lowest maximum local interfacial current in the calculated current density distributions (Supplementary Fig. 1). Therefore, as in our previous investigation of plating, the egg-box topography was considered further29.

The egg-box topography is parameterized by peak height (H) and peak separation (S) (Fig. 1c). The experimentally determined CCS for a range of egg-box topographies with varying H and S is shown in Fig. 1d. X-ray computed tomography (XCT) virtual cross sections of the egg-box interface with various combinations of H and S are shown in Supplementary Fig. 3. The highest CCS is observed for peaks that are low in height and close together. This is consistent with the modelling, described in Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Fig. 4, the results of which are presented in Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 5 and discussed below.

White and black dashed lines in a and c indicate the corresponding values for a non-contoured interface.

Several factors may influence void formation at contoured interfaces, such as the local current density, pressure and Li flux. Although a comprehensive model of voiding is beyond the scope of the present work, we consider here how each of these factors is affected at the bottom of the troughs, where voids initiate across a range of contour dimensions. Compared with a flat interface, contouring increases the surface area and therefore reduces the overall current density (Supplementary Fig. 5a). Egg-box contours with small peak separation generally exhibit lower current density at the bottom of the troughs, reducing the driving force for void formation (Fig. 2a). Considering pressure, contoured surfaces that provide greater pressure gradients towards the bottom of the troughs will enhance creep and thus mitigate void formation (Supplementary Fig. 5b). This occurs when the pressures in the troughs are positive tending to zero. Consequently, all contoured combinations with lower trough pressures are expected to better resist void growth (Fig. 2b). Furthermore, the Li flux towards the troughs is enhanced at contoured compared with planar interfaces, analogous to how microelectrodes enhance mass transport in liquid electrochemistry32,33 (Supplementary Fig. 5c). The higher the flux towards the trough, the lower the concentration of vacancies at the base of the trough. As shown in Fig. 2c, greater flux to the trough (lower vacancy concentration) will occur for lower peak heights. Higher curvature enhances the local flux, but increasing peak height lengthens the diffusion path, which turns out to be the more important effect. Together these factors describe complementary aspects of the same process: the local current density sets the rate at which Li is removed at the trough, while pressure and Li flux determine the rate at which it is replenished from within the metal. The combined effect of current, pressure and Li flux in the troughs is shown by overlapping Fig. 2a–c in Fig. 2d. Only a subset of the contoured interfaces benefits from all three factors. They have small peaks relatively close together, consistent with the experimentally measured CCS results (Fig. 2e). Finer features could not be investigated because of the resolution limit of the 3D printing. At sufficiently small contour dimensions, approaching the scale of intrinsic electrolyte surface defects, the interfacial current distribution is expected to become dominated by stochastic surface defects rather than the controlled contour geometry. The lower limit of the contoured regime may therefore ultimately be set by the electrolyte surface defect population.

Following these findings, an egg-box topography with a peak height of 5 µm and a peak separation of 30 µm was selected for further study.

Constant current discharge

Figure 3 shows the results of cycling the contoured Li/SE interface under various conditions, with each case compared to the same conditions for the non-contoured interface. The non-contoured interface was formed by pressing Argyrodite electrolyte powder with flat 3D-printed polymer discs within a die set. Both contoured and non-contoured electrolytes exhibit similar defect densities near the electrolyte interface (Supplementary Fig. 6 and Supplementary Table 1). Li was pressed onto the contoured and non-contoured surfaces. In each case, the cell was first plated at 0.2 mA cm−2 for 1 mAh cm−2 and the cycled areal capacity was also 1 mAh cm−2. Figure 3a–c presents results collected at 30 °C. At a 7 MPa stack pressure, the contoured interface could sustain repeated cycles with discharge current densities of 4 mA cm−2 without appreciable polarization (<2 mV; Fig. 3a, left). By contrast, the non-contoured interface shows polarization during the first stripping, which increases on cycling indicating void accumulation (Fig. 3a, right). At 2 MPa and 30 °C, the highest discharge current that can be stably cycled using a contoured interface is 2 mA cm−2 (Fig. 3b, left). At atmospheric pressures (0.1 MPa), the highest discharge current possible is 0.5 mA cm−2 (Fig. 3c, left). At both 2 and 0.1 MPa, the non-contoured cells polarized drastically on the first stripping (Fig. 3b,c, right). Interestingly, remaining at atmospheric pressure but increasing the temperature to 60 °C raises the maximum discharge current density for the contoured interface to 4 mA cm−2, whereas the non-contoured interface shows very severe polarization on stripping (Fig. 3d). Increasing the pressure to 2 MPa at 60 °C then further elevates this to 6 mA cm−2 (Fig. 3e, left).

Within each panel, results for the egg-box-contoured interface (peak height of 5 µm, peak separation of 30 µm) are shown on the left and those for non-contoured interface on the right. a, Under 7 MPa at 30 °C with a stripping current of 4 mA cm−2. b, Under 2 MPa at 30 °C with a stripping current of 2 mA cm−2. c, Under 0.1 MPa at 30 °C with a stripping current of 0.5 mA cm−2. d, Under 0.1 MPa at 60 °C with a stripping current of 4 mA cm−2. e, Under 2 MPa at 60 °C with a stripping current of 6 mA cm−2. Cycling of the three-electrode Li/Li6PS5Cl cells was carried out using a low plating current of 0.2 mA cm−2 in all cases to avoid dendrites during plating. For all cells, an areal capacity of 1 mAh cm−2 is moved per half cycle.

The results in Fig. 3 represent the maximum stripping currents for the contoured interfaces under each condition, as confirmed by Supplementary Fig. 7, which shows that any further increase in stripping current will result in appreciable polarization. Non-contoured interfaces can only cycle with a maximum discharge current density of 0.1 mA cm−2 at 2 MPa and 30 °C, and 0.3 mA cm−2 at 0.1 MPa and 60 °C without substantial polarization (Supplementary Fig. 8). Comparing Fig. 3 with Supplementary Fig. 8 shows that at low pressures contouring can enable an order of magnitude improvement in stable stripping current densities.

summary: Discharge-induced voids are a major barrier to practical lithium metal solid-state batteries.
